title: Replace Nested Loops with Lookups
content: Nested loops over two collections cost O(n*m) steps, often to match items between them. Build a dict or set from one collection once, then loop over the other and look up matches in O(1). Instead of `for a in orders: for c in customers: if a.cid == c.id`, build `by_id = {c.id: c for c in customers}` and use `by_id.get(a.cid)`. Fewer CPU steps means less energy.

title: Use Sets or Dicts for Membership Tests
content: `x in some_list`, `list.index(x)` and `list.count(x)` scan the whole list each time (O(n)). Inside a loop this becomes O(n^2). Convert the list to a set or dict once before the loop so each lookup is O(1) on average. Use `collections.Counter` instead of calling `.count()` for every item.

title: Hoist Loop-Invariant Work Out of Loops
content: Work that gives the same result on every iteration, such as `len(data)`, `sorted(items)`, `sum(values)`, `math.sqrt(2)`, `set(allowed)` or a config lookup, is loop-invariant. Compute it once before the loop and store it in a local variable. Repeating the same computation on every pass wastes CPU cycles.

title: Use Comprehensions Instead of Append Loops
content: A loop whose only job is `result.append(expr)` is slower than a list comprehension `[expr for x in items]`, which runs in optimized bytecode without repeated method lookups. The same applies to dict and set comprehensions. For simple transforms, built-ins like `map` or `filter` are also fine.

title: Build Strings with str.join
content: String concatenation with `s += piece` or `s = s + piece` in a loop can copy the whole string on every iteration, because strings are immutable. This is O(n^2) in the worst case. Collect pieces in a list and call `''.join(pieces)` once, or write to `io.StringIO`.

title: Prefer Built-in Functions Over Manual Loops
content: Built-ins such as `sum`, `min`, `max`, `sorted`, `any`, `all`, `enumerate`, `zip` and `collections.Counter` are implemented in C and do the same work as hand-written Python loops with far fewer interpreter steps. Replace manual accumulator loops (`total = 0; for x in xs: total += x`) with the matching built-in.

title: Use Generators for One-Pass Aggregation
content: `sum([x * x for x in xs])` builds a full list in memory before summing. `sum(x * x for x in xs)` streams values without the temporary list. With `any()` and `all()`, a generator also stops early as soon as the answer is known, while a list comprehension always computes every item.

title: Cache Results of Repeated Pure Function Calls
content: Recursive functions like naive Fibonacci call themselves with the same arguments many times, which grows exponentially. Decorate deterministic functions with `functools.lru_cache` or `functools.cache`, or rewrite them iteratively. The same applies to any expensive pure function called repeatedly with the same inputs.

title: Open Files Once, Not Inside Loops
content: Opening, reading or writing a file inside a loop repeats system calls and disk access on every iteration. Open the file once outside the loop, read what you need once, and batch writes (for example `f.writelines(lines)` or one `f.write('\n'.join(lines))`). Always use `with` so the file is closed promptly.

title: Stream Large Files Instead of Loading Them Whole
content: `f.read()` and `f.readlines()` load the whole file into memory. For large files iterate over the file object line by line (`for line in f:`) or read fixed-size chunks. This keeps peak memory low and avoids swapping.

title: Compile Regular Expressions Once
content: Calling `re.search`, `re.match`, `re.sub` or `re.findall` with a pattern string inside a loop re-checks the pattern cache every time, and `re.compile` inside a loop recompiles it. Compile the pattern once with `re.compile` outside the loop and reuse the compiled object.

title: Vectorize Numeric Work with NumPy
content: Python loops over large numeric arrays run one element at a time in the interpreter. NumPy operations such as `arr * 2`, `arr.sum()` or `np.dot(a, b)` run in compiled code with SIMD instructions and use far less CPU time. Only worth it when the data is large and NumPy is already a dependency.

title: Avoid Row-by-Row Iteration in Pandas
content: `DataFrame.iterrows()` and `itertuples()` loops, and `apply` with a Python function per row, are much slower than vectorized column operations such as `df['a'] * df['b']`, `df.groupby(...).sum()` or `np.where(...)`. Rewrite row loops as column expressions.

title: Sort Once and Use heapq or bisect
content: Sorting inside a loop repeats O(n log n) work. Sort once before the loop. To get the top k items use `heapq.nlargest(k, items)` instead of sorting everything. To keep a list sorted while inserting, use `bisect.insort` instead of appending and re-sorting.

title: Use deque for Queue Operations
content: `list.pop(0)` and `list.insert(0, x)` shift every element, which is O(n) per call. Use `collections.deque` with `popleft()` and `appendleft()`, which are O(1). This matters for queues and breadth-first search.

title: Avoid Unnecessary Copies of Data
content: Slicing (`items[1:]`), `list(x)`, `copy.deepcopy` and `+` on lists create new copies. Inside loops or recursion this multiplies memory use and CPU work. Pass indexes instead of slices, iterate directly over the original, and copy only when you truly need an independent object.

title: Exit Loops Early When the Answer Is Known
content: A search loop that keeps going after it finds its match wastes work. Use `break`, `return`, `any()`, or `next((x for x in xs if cond(x)), None)` to stop as soon as the result is known. Put cheap conditions before expensive ones in `and`/`or` expressions.

title: Batch Database Queries and Select Only Needed Columns
content: Running one query per item inside a loop (the N+1 query problem) multiplies round trips. Fetch related rows in one query with `WHERE id IN (...)` or a join, write with `executemany` or bulk inserts, and select only the columns you use instead of `SELECT *`.

title: Reuse Network Connections and Batch Requests
content: Creating a new HTTP connection for every request repeats TCP and TLS handshakes. Reuse a `requests.Session()` or `httpx.Client()`, call batch endpoints when the API offers them, and avoid calling the same URL repeatedly for data that does not change.

title: Reduce Output and Logging in Hot Loops
content: Calling `print` or logging on every iteration of a large loop turns cheap work into slow I/O. Collect results and print once, print a summary, or log at debug level with lazy arguments (`logger.debug('value %s', v)`) so disabled messages are never formatted.

title: Serialize and Parse Data Once
content: Calling `json.loads`, `json.dumps` or similar parsers on the same data inside a loop repeats expensive work. Parse once, keep the Python object, and serialize once at the end. For large data exchange, compact binary formats (for example MessagePack or Parquet) use less CPU and space than text JSON.
